tier_reason: Numbers are real (benchmarks.tex: Asio 29.5 s, Tokio 30.7 s, Go 35.6 s, Libuv 43.6 s, Nodejs 74.2 s) and server code is public (benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go, benchmarks/c/libuv/echo_server_direct.c, benchmarks/cpp/asio/echo_server_client.cpp), but there is no CPU model or Go version, each bar is one run recorded on a different date (libuv by 2022-07-15, Go 2022-08-25 after a server rewrite), and the C side is the libuv docs example that mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer and a write request per message at -O2 while Go reuses one 1 KiB buffer: crippled-baseline and cross-run precedents put the Go-over-C claim at D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Go 35.6 s vs libuv 43.6 s wall time for 1000 connections x 5000 echoes (about 1.22x less wall time, derived from page data); Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 1.21x faster than Go (derived from page data). Each value is a single run; the Go value was recorded on 2022-08-25 after the Go server was rewritten (it was 81.0 s before), the libuv value by 2022-07-15. Doc text: 'Go did surprise me: faster than nodejs and libuv!'
corrections.compiler_and_flags: libuv server: 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2 -o echo_server_direct' (benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md), linked against an unstated system libuv build. Go server: version and build command not stated; runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1), one goroutine per connection, 1024-byte buffer. Asio server/client: CMake target with C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler and optimisation level not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart on the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' (doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc); the rendered PNG on boostorg.github.io was not viewed. The chart is a composite of single `time` runs recorded on different dates by the Boost.Redis (C++) author on 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms; no CPU model, OS, Go/Rust/compiler versions, no repetitions or variance): libuv 43.568 s was recorded by 2022-07-15 (commit 3fb018c) and never re-run; Tokio moved from 42.2 s/43.2 s to 30.7 s on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime; Go moved from 81.0 s to 35.6 s on 2022-08-25 (commit f11622e) after its server was rewritten from bufio ReadBytes line echo to a raw 1024-byte read loop with GOMAXPROCS(1); Asio was re-measured at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07. Unequal work: the libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example, which mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer (libuv passes 64*1024 as suggested_size, src/unix/stream.c) on every read callback and a write_req_t per echo and frees both after each write, while the Go, Tokio and Asio servers reuse one 1 KiB buffer per connection; the Go server was revised between runs, the libuv one never was. The libuv server is built per benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md with 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2' (not -O3; system libuv build flags unknown). The load generator is the single-threaded Boost.Asio echo_server_client (1000 sessions x 5000 13-byte ping-pong messages) on the same host, which may set a floor near the Asio/Tokio results. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, Tokio current_thread, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. The author gives no explanation for the gap beyond 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio'. The Go server ignores conn.Write's return value (its error check tests the stale read error), harmless for timing. Measured in 2022 (Go about 1.19); the doc page is unchanged since.
corrections.why_faster: Not explained by the author. From the sources: the C (libuv) server allocates and frees a 64 KiB read buffer and a write request for every message (likely heap churn and possibly brk trimming; not measured), while Go reuses one 1 KiB buffer per goroutine over its epoll-based netpoller; the C server is also built at -O2. An Asio C++ server with the same reused-buffer design is faster than Go, so the gap is the libuv example's implementation, not the language.

notes: Downgrade C to D: the only C baseline Go beats is the unmodified libuv docs example (per-message 64 KiB malloc plus write-request malloc, -O2) recorded weeks before the revised Go server, one run each; Go loses to the C++ Asio server (29.5 s) in the same table. Shortcomings for decisions.json: composite single-run chart across July-October 2022, no hardware or versions, unequal buffer management, -O2 C build, single-threaded client may cap results.

tier_reason: First-party student report (graphs; the only quoted timings, Mandelbrot view 1 Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms and 18758.684 ms after the Complex32 fix, match) with raw timings in data/Data.xlsx and C++ Makefiles at g++ -m64 -O3 -fopenmp, but no CPU model, no Rust build flags or rustc version, the C++ sort source is not committed, and the matmul baseline kernel computes a different product; C at best.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed; absolute times from data/Data.xlsx (best of three). Matmul 2048x2048, Rayon par_chunks row-dot vs OpenMP: Rust faster at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12 and 16 threads (12 threads 2168.8 vs 2864.5 ms, about 1.32x; 16 threads 2149.1 vs 2264.2 ms, about 1.05x, derived from page data) but slower at 8 threads (2501.7 vs 2277.6 ms) and serially (16277.1 vs 15509.5 ms); the report's 'Rayon performs better for all cases of threads for size 2048' is contradicted by its own 8-thread row, and its 'C++ is faster for all cases of threads for size 1024' by the 12-thread (272.4 vs 362.1 ms) and 16-thread (265.2 vs 285.7 ms) rows. These matmul comparisons are invalid (see caveats). Stable parallel sort, 100M elements: Rayon par_sort 1380 ms vs GNU parallel stable sort 1534.1 ms at 12 threads and 1226 vs 1476.2 ms at 16 threads (about 1.11x and 1.20x, derived from page data); C++ faster at 1 to 8 threads (8 threads 1690.0 vs 1834 ms) and serially (8467.6 vs 10908 ms). Unstable sort: Rust pdqsort/par_sort_unstable is faster in absolute time at every thread count (100M serial 3611 vs 7851.1 ms; 16 threads 684 vs 975.4 ms) although the report says C++ scales better; this is pdqsort vs introsort/multiway mergesort, an algorithm difference. Mandelbrot: C++ faster serially and Rust within about 1% multithreaded; quoted serial view 1 (4096x4096): Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms, Rust 18758.684 ms after removing the num::Complex32 overhead. Reduction: Rust marginally faster serially (500M sum 456.5 vs 460.5 ms), OpenMP faster at every thread count.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ -m64 -O3 -Wall -fopenmp (C++/mandelbrot, matrixmultiply, quicksort, reduction Makefiles; no -march); the committed C++ quicksort binary's .comment reads 'GCC: (GNU) 4.8.5 20150623 (Red Hat 4.8.5-36)'. Rust: Cargo.toml files have no [profile] section; build command (release or not) and rustc version not stated; Rayon 1.0.3.
corrections.caveats: Student course project (CMU 15-618, 2019): results are graphs inside a PDF plus raw timings in data/Data.xlsx; no hardware stated (threads swept to 16); no license file. Harness defects found in the committed code: (1) the C++ matmul kernels matmul_serial2 and matmul_par_row compute c += A[iOff + k] * B[RM(k, i, size)], indexing B by the row i instead of the column j, so C++ computes a different (wrong) product whose B working set is a single cache-resident column per row, while the Rust kernel correctly walks B[index][col]; the bug is masked because A and B are all ones and the C++ result is never verified, so the matmul comparison is not same-work; (2) the C++ 'par_outer' timing block calls matmul_par_row again and never resets minThread, so the par_outer rows duplicate par_row; (3) the C++ sort source (C++/quicksort/main.cpp) is not committed, only a prebuilt ELF binary whose symbols show std::vector<int> (32-bit keys) sorted with __gnu_parallel multiway mergesort, while the Rust benchmark sorts Vec<u64> (64-bit keys), so element widths differ (against Rust); (4) the committed Rust sort code times stable_sort_par in its 'unstable parallel' loop (unstable_sort_par, typed &mut [u32], is never called) and prints fractional milliseconds, whereas Data.xlsx holds integer-millisecond Rust sort times that differ between stable and unstable, so the Rust sort numbers came from an earlier, uncommitted code version; correctness asserts are commented out; (5) Data.xlsx has copy errors (Rust Mandelbrot view 1 row-parallel row duplicates view 0). The Rayon matmul advantage the report explains (Rust not vectorizing the inner loop and hitting the compute limit later, par_chunks avoiding fork-join overhead) rests on the invalid kernel comparison. Sort compares different library algorithms (Rust stable merge sort and pdqsort vs GNU parallel multiway mergesort and introsort). Old toolchains: GCC 4.8.5 (2015) vs Rayon 1.0.3-era rustc (2019).
corrections.workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images, 7 views), integer matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square, all-ones inputs), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rust: uniform random u64 via par_sort/par_sort_unstable; C++: std::vector<int> via GNU parallel mode, source not committed), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, threads 1 to 16.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language win. Matmul: invalid comparison (C++ kernel indexes B[k][i], a different and wrong product). Stable sort at 12-16 threads: Rayon's parallel merge sort (tuned merge variants per the report) vs libstdc++ parallel-mode multiway mergesort from GCC 4.8.5, despite Rust sorting 64-bit keys vs 32-bit. Unstable sort: pdqsort vs introsort, an algorithm difference.

notes: Keep at tier C but the claim was overstated: the matmul win is invalid because the C++ kernel indexes B by row i (wrong, cache-friendlier product, masked by all-ones inputs), the report's 2048 'every thread count' claim fails at 8 threads, the C++ sort source is missing (binary only, 32-bit ints vs Rust u64), and the committed Rust sort code is not the version that produced the numbers. The only surviving Rayon-over-OpenMP result is stable parallel sort at 12-16 threads (about 1.11-1.20x at 100M, derived). Usability reference (no license), abandoned (last commit 2019-11-01).
